study.title: Isaiah 61 - Consolation, Restoration, and righteousness before the nations
study.overview: Isaiah 61 presents a message of total restoration: the envoy of God announces good news to the broken, reversal of shame, reconstruction of what was destroyed, and formation of a people identified by justice and praise. The notes link the passage to the mission of the Servant/Messiah and also to the restoration of the people of God after distress. The chapter moves from the proclamation of salvation to its visible effects: healing, joy, reconstruction, ordained service, renewed honor and secure fruitfulness, culminating in the certainty that the Lord Himself will bring forth justice and praise among the nations.

outline.title: The anointed announces liberation and reversal of pain
outline.explanation: The opening verses describe someone empowered by the Spirit of the Lord to proclaim good news, healing, and deliverance. The notes highlight that Jesus applied these words to his mission, and also show the contrast between grief and joy: ashes, sorrow and downcast spirit are exchanged for ornament, oil of joy and garments of praise.

outline.title: Restored ruins and a people with a priestly vocation
outline.explanation: Here the restoration becomes concrete: ruined places are rebuilt and foreigners begin to serve in daily work. Instead of marginality, the people are called priests of the Lord, receiving dignity, sustenance and a public identity of service to God.

outline.title: shame converted into inheritance and testimony among the nations
outline.explanation: Humiliation is exchanged for lasting joy and folded portion, abundant language of restoration. The Lord says that he loves righteousness and makes an everlasting covenant, so that the offspring of his people become known as the blessed people before the nations.

outline.title: Thanksgiving and certainty of divine fruiting
outline.explanation: The people's response is intense joy in the Lord, who dress them with salvation and justice as garments of feast and honor. The conclusion uses the image of the earth and the garden to affirm that the Lord will bring forth justice and praise in a visible and public way among all nations.

study.context: The notes interpret the chapter in connection with the restoration of the people of God after the oppression and the mission of Jesus Christ, who read the passage and applied it to himself. Thus, the text can be read on two related levels: the historical hope of restoration for Zion and the broader fulfillment in salvation brought by the Messiah. The explicit background in the notes is the contrast between shame, lamentation and ruin, and the divine intervention that reverses this condition.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that salvation is born from God's initiative and is accompanied by his Spirit; it is not mere social improvement, but integral redemption. The Lord's envoy brings good news to the poor and wounded, showing that divine mercy reaches the marginalized. At the same time, there is judgment: the favorable day of God is also a day of vengeance against the enemies of his people, which preserves divine justice. The restoration does not end in inner comfort; it produces a visible, reconstructed community, called to reflect the character of God himself, who loves justice and rejects evil. The eternal covenant and blessed offspring point to a stable, faithful and public work. Finally, the image of righteousness and praise sprang up as vegetation states that true renewal is the work of the Lord and becomes recognizable before the nations.

scholarViews.insight: Isaiah's words about the anointed were applied by the Lord Jesus to his own mission, showing that the good news includes healing of the broken and restoration of the marginalized.
The promises of rebuilding the ruins can be applied to the church and to the freed believers of spiritual slavery, as a continuation of the restoration announced to God's people.
The image of the chapter concludes with the certainty of prophecy: the Lord brings forth justice and praise as the earth brings forth its new ones, illustrating the firmness of the divine promise.

questions: How does the message of deliverance and healing in Isaiah 61 confront our expectations about how God acts in the midst of suffering?
In what respects can the church today reflect the identity of 'Lord's priests without confusing it with human prestige?
How can the promise that God bring forth justice and praise may sustain a community that still faces shame, ruin or prolonged waiting?
study.practice: Pray that the Spirit of the Lord may apply the promise of Isaiah 61 to his heart and community. Practice a faith that unites comfort and justice: welcome the wounded, participate in the reconstruction of what is broken and alive so that praise to God is visible. When there is shame, mourning or a sense of loss, remember that the Lord not only consoles, but also has salvation and justice. In concrete terms, choose an attitude this week that incarnates restoration: visiting someone down, serving in the recovery of a practical need or encouraging reconciliation and hope.
study.uncertainty: The chapter admits prophetic reading applied to the Messiah and also to the restoration of Israel, but the given notes do not authorize precisely defining all the historical stages of his fulfillment. There are also textual variations mentioned by Adam Clarke in specific verses, but with no sufficient basis here to safely conclude on the original text in every detail. Therefore, confessional interpretations were presented as possible readings and not as indisputable statements of the text.
